title: Scaling Laws: With 10x more compute, how much bigger should the model get? The three power laws
summary: The paper finds that language model loss falls smoothly with parameters, data, and compute according to power laws, while architectural details barely matter. We unpack the power laws, the 6N compute formula, the overfitting formula, and the optimal allocation, work through several tables by hand, then look at how the paper shows its own laws must eventually break down—and what Chinchilla later changed.
ai_summary: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (OpenAI, 2020) trained Transformers ranging from under a thousand to 1.5 billion parameters and found that test loss falls as a power law with parameter count N, dataset size D, and compute C, with exponents of about 0.076, 0.095, and 0.050, respectively. Depth, width, and other shape choices matter little. Overfitting depends only on N^{0.74}/D: scale the model 8x and about 5x more data is enough. Under fixed compute, optimal model size grows as C^{0.73}, training steps barely change, and training should stop about 10% above convergence. The paper also notes that its laws become self-contradictory around 10^{12} parameters. In 2022, Chinchilla revised the model-to-data allocation ratio.
brief: Question: Does language model performance come from scale or architecture? Given a budget, how big should the model be, how much data should you use, and how many training steps should you run?
Method: Train many Transformers of different sizes, shapes, and data volumes on WebText2, then fit the loss with power laws.

Result: Loss falls smoothly as a power law with parameters, data, and compute; architecture barely matters. Larger models are more data-efficient, and compute should go mostly toward larger models with early stopping.
Limitations: These are empirical laws with no theory; fixed training length and learning-rate schedules favor large models. In 2022, Chinchilla revised the conclusion to scale model and data in sync.

paper.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
paper.authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Dario Amodei

cover.headline: A close read of the Scaling Laws paper

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In January 2020, ten OpenAI authors (first author Jared Kaplan was then also at Johns Hopkins University) published this 30-page paper. It didn't propose a new model; it asked a more basic question: what actually determines how good a language model is, and can that be computed in advance?

They trained a large number of Transformer language models, the smallest with fewer than a thousand parameters and the largest with 1.5 billion, then plotted performance on log axes. The result was strikingly clean: as long as no other factor bottlenecks it, the model's loss (lower is better) falls along a straight line with parameter count N, dataset size D, and training compute C. That relationship is called a power law, and some trends span more than seven orders of magnitude. By comparison, whether the model is deeper or wider, or how many attention heads it has, barely matters.

From these laws, the paper made an influential recommendation: when you have more compute, spend most of it making the model bigger. For every 10x more compute, scale the model up about 5x and the data only about 2x. The most economical approach is to train a very large model and stop well before it has fully "learned." GPT-3 (175 billion parameters), released four months later, was built in this spirit; several of the paper's authors were also GPT-3 authors.

The paper's conclusions were later revised: DeepMind's 2022 Chinchilla paper found that data should grow roughly as fast as model size. But the core discovery—loss can be predicted ahead of time with power laws—has held, and today labs run small-scale experiments like these to extrapolate before training large models.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: A language model's test loss L falls as a power law with parameter count N, dataset size D, and compute C: L ∝ N^{−0.076}, D^{−0.095}, C^{−0.050}. Architecture barely matters; scale does. Larger models are more data-efficient; under a fixed compute budget, spend most of it on bigger models and don't train to convergence.

callout.title: Four small concepts you need for this paper
callout.text: You don't need to go deep on them; these four will do:
list: **Loss (cross-entropy)**: how "surprised" the model is when predicting the next token. Perfect prediction gives 0; the more uncertain it is, the larger the loss. The paper uses nats (natural logarithms); on this paper's data, good models score between 2 and 3.
**Log scale**: an axis where 1, 10, 100, and 1000 sit at equal intervals. On such a plot, a power law is a straight line—which is how all the paper's key figures are drawn.
**Parameter count N**: the number of trainable numbers in the model. This paper deliberately does not count token or positional embeddings; we'll see why below.
**Floating-point operations and PF-days**: units for measuring compute. One PF-day is 10^15 operations per second sustained for a day, about 8.64 × 10^{19} operations.

sections.h: The question: why do models actually get better?

blocks.p: By 2019, language models were improving quickly: GPT-2, BERT, and others were approaching human-level performance on many tasks. But the reason for the improvement was unclear: was it larger models, more data, longer training, or cleverer architectures? Every new paper changed several things at once, making the factors hard to separate.

This matters in practice. Training a large model costs enormous compute, and before you start you want to know: given the budget, how big should the model be? How much data should you prepare? How many steps should you run? Without a pattern to follow, you either guess or run the experiment first.

The paper chose a deliberately simple metric: cross-entropy loss on the WebText2 test set. The rationale is that it is continuous and comparable, and can be measured from very small models to the largest models of the era, so trends can be observed across many orders of magnitude. The tradeoff is that lower loss doesn't guarantee better real-task performance—a caveat the paper itself flags at the end.

callout.title: Like physicists studying gases
callout.text: The paper offers an analogy: these laws are like the ideal gas law. A gas contains countless molecules with wildly different details, yet pressure, volume, and temperature obey a simple relationship that barely depends on what the molecules look like. The authors hope to find the "macroscopic laws" of language models; as for the underlying "statistical mechanics," the paper admits it doesn't yet know.

sections.h: What a power law is: every doubling multiplies loss by a fixed factor

blocks.p: A power law has the form L = (X_{c} / X)^{α}: X is scale (parameters, data, or compute), X_{c} is a constant, and α is the exponent. Its most direct meaning: every time X grows by a factor of k, loss multiplies by k^{−α}, no matter what scale you're at.

For parameters, the paper measures α_N ≈ 0.076. Doubling parameters multiplies loss by 2^{−0.076} ≈ 0.95, a drop of about 5%. Multiplying parameters by 10 multiplies loss by 10^{−0.076} ≈ 0.84, a drop of about 16%. The ratio is the same at a thousand parameters and a billion.

parts.desc: The test loss of a model with N parameters, trained to convergence on enough data
A scale constant. Its value depends on the vocabulary and tokenization, and has no meaning in itself
The exponent; it determines how much benefit a larger model brings. 0.076 is small, meaning you have to scale the model up a lot to see clear improvement

formula.note: Take logarithms on both sides: log L = α_{N} · (log N_{c} − log N). So on log axes, log L versus log N is a straight line with slope −α_{N}.

plain.title: Every doubling applies a fixed discount
plain.text: On linear axes, a power law is a curve that keeps flattening out (left), as if each step helps less. On log axes (right), it becomes a straight line: every doubling of parameters multiplies loss by 0.95, no matter where the doubling starts. Because the line can be extended, small models can be used to predict large ones.

fig.title: Using the formula: every 10x more parameters lowers loss about 16%
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: calculated from the paper's Equation 1.1, not measured data; loss is in nats/token. The amber row marks GPT-2's scale (about 1.5 billion parameters).
fig.note: This formula only holds when the model is bottlenecked by parameters: data must be plentiful and training long enough. The largest model actually tested in the paper is about 1.5 billion parameters, so the 10-billion row is already an extrapolation.

callout.title: Power laws are not "bigger is always better, without end"
callout.text: Two things are true at once. First, each 10x increase only reduces loss about 16%, so the absolute drop shrinks: from 4.02 to 3.37 is a drop of 0.65, while from 2.38 to 1.99 is only 0.39. That's diminishing returns. Second, language has its own uncertainty—many plausible tokens can follow the same prefix—so loss can never reach 0, and the straight line must eventually flatten. The paper says it saw no sign of flattening within its experimental range, but it will happen.

blocks.p: Why a power law rather than some other curve? The appendix compares logarithmic and other forms, and the power law fits clearly better. As for the theoretical reason, the paper admits there is no solid understanding yet. It notes that similar power laws appear in density estimation, random forests, and other models, and offers a rough interpretation: the exponent roughly corresponds to the inverse of the number of "useful features" in the data.

quiz.q: The parameter exponent is α_N ≈ 0.076. If you scale a model from 100 million parameters to 1 billion, what roughly happens to test loss?
options: It drops to one-tenth of its original value
quiz.why: A 10x increase multiplies loss by 10^{−0.076} ≈ 0.84, so it drops about 16%. One-tenth would mean mistaking the power law for inverse proportionality; "drops by 0.076" mistakes the exponent for an absolute change in loss.

sections.h: How the experiments worked: many models, one dataset

blocks.p: All models were trained on WebText2, an extended version of the WebText dataset used for GPT-2. It collects outbound Reddit links with at least 3 karma, extended through October 2018. In total it contains 20.3 million documents and 96 GB of text, tokenized with GPT-2's tokenizer into about 22.9 billion tokens; 660 million of those are held out as a test set. The paper also evaluates on Books Corpus, Common Crawl, English Wikipedia, and a collection of internet books to check whether models transfer to other text.

The factors varied included model size (non-embedding parameters from 768 to 1.5 billion), data volume (22 million to 23 billion tokens), shape (layers, width, attention heads, feed-forward width), context length, and batch size. The default setup used the Adam optimizer, a fixed 2.5 × 10^{5} training steps, batches of 512 sequences of 1024 tokens, and a learning rate that rises linearly for 3000 steps then cosine-decays to 0; models above 1 billion parameters switched to Adafactor due to memory constraints.

**How parameter count is computed.** A Transformer layer mostly consists of the attention and feed-forward weight matrices. Ignoring biases and other small terms, the non-embedding parameter count is:

formula.expr: N ≈ 2 · d_{model} · n_{layer} · ( 2 d_{attn} + d_{ff} ) = 12 · n_{layer} · d_{model}^{2}

parts.desc: the dimension of each token vector (the width of the residual stream)
attention output dimension, usually equal to d_{model}
the intermediate width of the feed-forward layer, usually 4 · d_{model}
Substituting the standard settings d_{attn} = d_{model} and d_{ff} = 4d_{model}: 2 × (2 + 4) = 12

formula.note: The attention layer has four d_{model} × d_{model} matrices—query, key, value, and output—totaling 4d_{model}^{2}; the feed-forward layer has two d_{model} × 4d_{model} matrices, totaling 8d_{model}^{2}. Together that is exactly 12d_{model}^{2} per layer.

plain.title: A layer is a handful of large matrices
plain.text: Each layer's parameters are mostly four d × d attention matrices plus two d × 4d feed-forward matrices—together, 12 d². Multiply by the number of layers, and you get the whole model's parameter count. If you know the layer count and width, you can estimate the model size in your head.

fig.title: Checking 12 · n_{layer} · d_{model}^{2} against two real models
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: layer counts and widths from the GPT-2 and GPT-3 papers; calculations by this site.
fig.note: The gap is mostly the embedding layer this paper deliberately excludes: GPT-3's vocabulary has more than 50,000 tokens, each with a 12,288-dimensional vector, adding up to over 600 million parameters.

blocks.p: **Why exclude the embedding layer?** The paper found that when embedding parameters are counted, models of different depths fall on different curves, making depth look important. Once embeddings are removed, models of varying depth collapse onto almost a single line; only models with fewer than 2 layers or extreme depth-to-width ratios clearly deviate. This suggests the embedding matrix can be made smaller without hurting performance.

**How compute is calculated.** In the forward pass, each parameter does about one multiply and one add per token, or 2N operations; the backward pass is about twice the forward pass. Training therefore takes about 6N floating-point operations per token, so total compute C ≈ 6N · B · S (B is tokens per batch, S is steps). This ignores context-dependent attention computation, which is small as long as d_{model} is much larger than one-twelfth of the context length.

callout.title: The 6N rule is surprisingly handy
callout.text: It lets you estimate training cost in your head. Take GPT-3: 175 billion parameters, trained on 300 billion tokens. 6 × 1.75 × 10^{11} × 3 × 10^{11} ≈ 3.15 × 10^{23} operations, or about 3650 PF-days. The GPT-3 paper itself reports 3.14 × 10^{23} operations and about 3640 PF-days—almost identical (this site's check using the formula). Today people still use the same equation to estimate the training cost of large models.

quiz.q: A Transformer has 24 layers and width d_{model} = 1024 (with standard d_{attn} and d_{ff}). Using the paper's formula, roughly how many non-embedding parameters does it have?
quiz.why: 12 × 24 × 1024² = 12 × 24 × 1,048,576 ≈ 302 million. That's the BERT-LARGE / GPT-2 Medium class (about 340 million with embeddings). 25 million comes from forgetting to multiply by the number of layers; 1.2 billion comes from multiplying by 12 twice.

sections.h: Finding 1: Architecture barely matters; scale does

blocks.p: The paper fixes non-embedding parameter count N and changes only one shape parameter at a time (adjusting width to keep N constant), then looks at the loss. The conclusion: across a wide range, loss changes by only a few percentage points.

list: **Depth-to-width ratio**: varying d_{model} / n_{layer} by a factor of 40 has little effect. A model with only 6 layers and width 4288 differs in loss from the 48-layer, width-1600 configuration used in GPT-2 by less than 3%.
**Attention head count and feed-forward width**: also barely matter within reasonable ranges.

**Compared with LSTM**: at the same parameter count, an LSTM matches the Transformer at the beginning of a text, but stops improving after about 100 tokens. The Transformer keeps getting more accurate across the whole 1024-token context. So the Transformer's advantage comes mainly from exploiting long context.

**Transfer to other text**: On Wikipedia, books, and Common Crawl, loss also falls smoothly with N, and the curves run almost parallel to the WebText2 curve, offset by a roughly constant amount. How well a model generalizes depends almost entirely on its loss on the training distribution, not on how long it trained or how deep it is.

blocks.p: The paper mentions one possible explanation: a deep network may behave like an ensemble of shallow networks (an idea earlier research proposed for ResNets), which would explain why depth makes little difference.

callout.title: 'Doesn't matter' has limits
callout.text: The claim is that shape matters little **within a reasonable range** and **at fixed parameter count**. A model with only one layer, or an extreme depth-to-width ratio, still gets clearly worse. The practical takeaway: when designing a large model, don't spend much effort on architectural details; get the scale right first.

sections.h: Finding 2: Three power laws for model, data, and compute

blocks.p: When only one factor is the bottleneck and the other two are plentiful, loss follows three clean power laws:

fig.title: The three power laws: the data exponent is largest, the compute exponent smallest
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Equations 1.1–1.3 and Appendix Table 5; the 'loss multiplier for 10x' column is computed by this site using 10^{−α}. Amber marks the compute row.
rows: Model large enough, stopped before overfitting
Optimally sized model, batch sufficiently small
fig.note: The scale constants depend on tokenization; change the tokenizer and their values change, so don't read physical meaning into them.

blocks.p: The compute exponent is the smallest, which makes it look like the worst deal: 10x more compute reduces loss by only about 11%. But compute is the fundamental budget—both N and D have to be bought with it. The central question of the paper's second half is: given a compute budget, how should you split it between model size and data to move along this C curve.

The paper also measured the **critical batch size**: how many tokens per batch is best. Too small, and the GPU is underutilized; above a critical value, larger batches only waste compute and barely reduce the number of steps. The critical value depends only on current loss, not model size, roughly B_{crit} ≈ 2.1 × 10^{8} · L^{−4.8} tokens: every time loss drops 13%, the critical batch size roughly doubles. For the largest models trained to convergence, it is about one to two million tokens.

plain.title: At some point, extra hands just get in each other's way
plain.text: In a move, three people are much faster than one; ten is faster still. Beyond that, the hallway gets jammed and the speed barely increases. Batch size works the same way: past the critical value B_crit, packing more data into each batch barely reduces the number of training steps—it just burns compute.

fig.title: The stronger the model, the more tokens a batch can hold
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: calculated from the paper's formula B_{crit} ≈ 2.1 × 10^{8} · L^{−4.8}, not measured data.
fig.note: The intuition: the better the model, the finer the remaining signal, so the 'noise' in each step's gradient is relatively larger and needs a bigger batch to average out. Blue marks a loss of about 3.0, roughly one million tokens.

sections.h: Finding 3: Model and data grow together—but data can grow more slowly

blocks.p: Scaling the model without adding data causes overfitting; adding data without scaling the model means the model can't absorb it. The paper found a single formula combining both that fits the experiments across simultaneous changes in N and D:

parts.desc: When data is infinite, the second term vanishes and this reduces to L(N): constrained only by model size.
When the model is infinite, the first term vanishes and this reduces to L(D): constrained only by dataset size.
The exponent on the first term is about 0.076 / 0.095 ≈ 0.8, ensuring both limits agree.

formula.note: The paper says it chose this form based on three principles: changing the vocabulary should only rescale loss; the two limits must match; and near infinite data, loss should be expandable in integer powers of 1/D. The authors admit the third has weaker theoretical support.

plain.title: Two pipes: the narrower one sets the flow
plain.text: Model size N and dataset size D are like two pipes feeding a funnel. Whichever is narrower limits the flow: a big model with little data overfits; lots of data with a small model can't be absorbed. The formula puts both bottlenecks together, and whichever is tighter mainly determines the loss.

blocks.p: From this, the paper calculates that **overfitting depends only on the ratio N^{0.74} / D** (0.74 ≈ 0.076 / 0.095). Plainly: **every time you scale the model 8x, you only need about 5x more data** (8^{0.74} ≈ 4.7) to avoid being hurt by a data shortage. This is a 'sublinear' relationship: data volume doesn't have to grow in proportion to parameters.
The paper estimates loss variation across random seeds at about 0.02. To keep the effect of overfitting below that fluctuation, data should satisfy D ≳ 5 × 10^{3} · N^{0.74} (in tokens):

fig.title: Using Equation 4.4: how much data do you need to avoid overfitting?
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: computed by this site from the paper's formula D ≳ 5 × 10^{3} · N^{0.74}; N excludes embedding parameters. The amber row matches the paper's experiments.
rows: Exactly WebText2's size: the paper says models under 1 billion parameters barely overfit on it
GPT-3 actually trained on about 300 billion tokens (different dataset, so only a rough comparison)

blocks.p: In the experiments, all models used 10% dropout and stopped early when test loss stopped improving. The fit was good, with one exception: the group where data was cut to about 20 million tokens had only 40 update steps per epoch, so overfitting happened too early and may fall into a different regime.

callout.title: The paper doesn't support 'data should match parameters'
callout.text: According to this paper, data only needs to grow as parameters to the 0.74 power, so larger models are more 'data-frugal.' This was one basis for the 2020-era preference for 'large model, relatively little data.' Two years later, Chinchilla reached a different conclusion (see the end), and this is also the point for which the paper is most often cited.

quiz.q: According to this paper's scaling law, when you increase model parameters 8x, by how much should data grow to avoid being hurt by too little data?
quiz.why: Overfitting depends only on N^{0.74} / D. To keep that ratio constant, D must be multiplied by 8^{0.74} ≈ 4.7, or about 5x. 8x is linear growth—the direction Chinchilla later took, not this paper's conclusion.

sections.h: Finding 4: Larger models learn faster, and training curves are predictable

blocks.p: The paper also fits loss as a function of **training steps**. With infinite data, after the initial unstable phase, the learning curve is:

parts.desc: The 'floor' set by model size: even infinite training can't go below it
The added loss from not training long enough, decaying as a power law in steps
Converted to the minimum steps required when 'the batch is large enough', used to cancel out the effect of different batch sizes

formula.note: This means you can look at the early part of a model's training curve and roughly predict its loss after much longer training.

plain.title: Larger models learn faster
plain.text: The three curves are models of three sizes (green is largest). At the dashed moment, all have seen the same amount of data, but the large model's loss is already far lower. Large models aren't 'slow and careful'; they learn more from every example.

blocks.p: Behind this formula is an important phenomenon: **larger models are more sample-efficient**. To reach the same loss, a larger model needs fewer training steps and less data. In the appendix, sample efficiency from the smallest to largest model differs by nearly 100x.

callout.title: Large models aren't 'slow and careful': they learn faster
callout.text: People often assume large models must be trained longer to pay off. The paper's chart shows the opposite: at the same number of tokens seen, a large model already has much lower loss than a small one. A large model learns more from each example. This is also the fundamental reason behind 'train a big model and stop early.'

blocks.p: The paper also examined loss at different positions in the context. At fixed model size, loss at token T falls as a power law in T. Large models are not only more accurate at the end; they also improve faster with very little context, which suggests they are better at quickly finding patterns. During training, models first learn short-range relationships and later learn long-range ones.

sections.h: The core conclusion: spend extra compute primarily on a bigger model

blocks.p: Now we can answer the most practical question: given a compute budget C, what's the best allocation? The paper substitutes C ≈ 6N · B · S into the learning-curve formula, solves for the model size that minimizes loss at fixed C, and compares with experiments. The experimental result is:

parts.desc: Optimal model size: grows fastest, absorbing most of the increase in compute
Batch size: grows with it; this part can be absorbed with more GPU parallelism
Training steps: barely grows with compute; the exponent 0.03 is small enough that it may be 0
Data seen = batch size × steps, growing roughly as C^{0.27}

formula.note: The theoretical value derived from the learning-curve formula is N ∝ C^{0.71}, within a few percentage points of the measured 0.73. The paper says this shows the whole set of laws can predict each other self-consistently.

plain.title: With a bigger budget, upgrade the kitchen before buying more groceries
plain.text: Compute is the total budget. In this paper's account, for every 10x more compute, most money should go to a bigger model (about 5x), data increases only a little (about 2x), and there's no need to train to the end. Two years later, Chinchilla revised the ratio, arguing model and data should grow at roughly the same rate.

fig.title: Every 10x more compute: model grows about 5x, data only about 2x
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: computed by this site from the paper's exponents 0.73, 0.27, 0.24, and 0.03. Blue column is model size.
fig.note: Figure 3 of the paper makes the same allocation for a 1-billion-fold increase in compute: most goes to model size, a little to data; within the data increase, most is absorbed by larger batches in parallel, while serial steps barely rise.

blocks.p: **Do not train to convergence.** By these laws, the most compute-efficient approach is to train a large model until its loss is about 10% above what it could ultimately reach—then stop (this ratio is exactly α_{N} / α_{S} ≈ 0.076 / 0.76). The paper compares this with common practice: if you train to within 2% of convergence, as people habitually do, then to reach the same loss you need a model 2.7x smaller but 7.7x more steps, which spends considerably more total compute. Conversely, the optimal approach **saves about 65% of compute**.

callout.title: Why 'big model, early stopping' is cheaper
callout.text: Training a model progresses fast early and slower later: that final sliver of loss costs a huge number of steps. Rather than squeezing the last bit out of a small model, it's better to switch to a larger model that learns faster and reaches the same position in fewer steps. An analogy: rather than making one person train from 90 to 98, hire someone who learns faster and stop them at 90—the latter's 90 is already better than the former's 98.

blocks.p: It's also fine if the model size isn't exactly right: the paper estimates that using 0.6x to 2.2x the optimal size costs only about 20% more compute. Slightly larger has an advantage: a 2.2x larger model needs 45% fewer steps, so if hardware is parallel enough, training is actually faster. Slightly smaller is cheaper at deployment (lower inference cost).

quiz.q: According to this paper, when a compute budget increases 10x, what should you increase most?
quiz.why: Optimal model size grows as C^{0.73}, so 10x compute means about 5x larger model; data grows only about C^{0.27} (about 2x), and serial steps barely change. 'All three in equal proportion' doesn't match this paper's conclusion; however, Chinchilla later argued model and data should grow at about the same rate.

quiz.q: A team fixes a compute budget and trains a medium-sized model until loss completely stops improving. According to this paper, what's wrong?
options: Nothing; training to convergence is always best
The model was too small: the same compute used to train a larger model and stop early would produce lower loss
The batch size is too large
quiz.why: One of the paper's core conclusions is that 'convergence is inefficient': the last stretch of loss reduction is very expensive. Spending that compute on a larger model instead already beats the converged smaller model at the same step count. The paper estimates the optimal approach saves about 65% of compute.

sections.h: The contradiction the paper itself found: the laws must eventually fail

blocks.p: The most interesting section of the paper is where it shows that its own laws start to conflict at larger scales.

list: **On one hand**, to avoid overfitting, data should grow with model size as D ∝ N^{0.74}; since the optimal model grows as N ∝ C^{0.73}, together these imply data should grow as about C^{0.54}.
**On the other hand**, training in the most compute-efficient way (each data point seen only once) uses data growing only about C^{0.26}, much more slowly.

**Result**: when compute is large enough, the optimally trained model hits a data wall. Under a data bottleneck, loss falls only about C^{−0.03}, slower than the C^{−0.050} of L(C_{min}); the two lines eventually cross, and beyond that point the L(C_{min}) prediction can no longer be realized.

plain.title: The two laws eventually collide
plain.text: The solid line is the loss achievable by 'training in the most compute-efficient way'; the dashed line is the lower bound from 'data seen only once', which falls much more slowly. The two curves eventually cross, and after that intersection the two laws cannot both hold. The paper guesses the intersection may be near the limit of such models, but it also says the numerical value is very uncertain.

fig.title: The intersection: the paper's guess at the limit of Transformer language models
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Equation 6.8. The paper stresses that these values are uncertain by an order of magnitude in either direction.
rows: about 3x GPT-3's training compute (this site's comparison)
possibly close to the 'entropy' of natural language per token

blocks.p: The most direct reading is that the laws will fail before this point is reached. But the paper also offers a bolder conjecture: if models cannot exceed N^{*} without changing the nature of the data, perhaps by then all reliable information in natural-language data has already been extracted, and L^{*} is a rough estimate of natural language's per-token entropy. The paper stresses this is only a conjecture.

callout.title: The paper has a few numbers that don't line up
list: **Orders of magnitude**: the abstract and Section 1.1 say the trends span 'more than seven orders of magnitude,' but the bullet list in the same section says 'more than six'; another spot says C_{min} spans eight orders, N six, and D a little over two.

**The compute exponent has three versions**: the empirical fit is 0.050; Section 6 derives a theoretical 0.054 from other exponents and the paper calls this 'very close'; Appendix B computes 0.052 using the same formula. This site's check with 1 / (1/0.76 + 1/0.21 + 1/0.076) gives 0.052.

**Scale constants don't match**: the fit label in Figure 13 is C_{min} / 2.3 × 10^{8}, but Equation 1.3 in the main text and Appendix Table 5 write 3.1 × 10^{8}; another fit label in Figures 1 and 13 is C / 2.0 × 10^{7}, while Appendix Table 5 gives 1.6 × 10^{7}.
**Leftover placeholders**: Appendix B.4 says "see Figure X" and "see Figure Y"—apparently the authors forgot to replace them with Figure 12.

**Two sets of parameters**: fitting L(D) alone gives α_{D} ≈ 0.095, while the joint fit of L(N, D) gives 0.103; N_{c} also changes from 8.8 × 10^{13} to 6.4 × 10^{13}. The paper explains this one itself: the two fits are to different equations.

blocks.p: The paper's appendix has a dedicated list of caveats:

list: **No theory**: the laws are empirical fits, and the model-size and compute laws are "especially mysterious." Without theory, it's hard to know when they can be trusted.
**The small-data regime is understudied**: the fit is poor when data is scarce, and the paper did not test regularization or data augmentation; those could change the conclusions.

**Hyperparameters left untuned**: the learning rate was tuned, but initialization scale, momentum, and others may not have been. Also, **the runs that stopped before convergence never tried larger learning rates.**
**The compute formula ignores context**: with very long contexts, C ≈ 6N underestimates compute.
**Critical batch extrapolation is unreliable**: far outside the experimental loss range, the B_{crit} prediction may not hold—and it affects the tradeoff between parallelism and training time.

**Loss is not capability**: at the end, the paper notes that smooth improvements in loss may hide qualitative changes in capability, just as smooth growth in total economic output hides the specific technological breakthroughs behind it.

blocks.p: **What came next.** Four months later, OpenAI released GPT-3: 175 billion parameters, trained on about 300 billion tokens—exactly the "large model, relatively little data, stop before convergence" playbook. The GPT-3 paper also used this paper's methods to plot the loss curve falling smoothly with scale (see our GPT-3 close read).

In 2022, DeepMind's Chinchilla paper ("Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models") re-examined this question and concluded that model and data should **grow at roughly the same rate**. The authors trained Chinchilla at 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens accordingly, and it outperformed a 280-billion-parameter Gopher trained with the same compute. Chinchilla identified one key difference: this paper gave every model the same training length and learning-rate schedule (a fixed 2.5 × 10^{5} steps, with cosine decay to zero). Under a schedule designed for long training, the intermediate checkpoints were never properly wound down, so their loss was overstated and the benefit of training on less data was understated. Chinchilla argues that this is one reason for the "model should grow faster than data" conclusion. In hindsight, that lands on a limitation the paper itself listed: it never tuned learning rates for runs that stopped short of convergence.

But the paper's most important legacy still stands: **before spending real money, fit power laws from a series of small models and extrapolate to large ones**. This has become standard practice before training large models. Chinchilla is also in your saved papers and will be our next close read.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you actually get it?

quiz.q: Why did the paper exclude the embedding layer when counting parameters?
options: Because the embedding layer has too few parameters to matter.
Because removing it makes models of different depths fall on the same power-law curve, giving a cleaner law.
Because the embedding layer isn't trained.
Because the compute formula doesn't include the embedding layer.
quiz.why: Figure 6 shows that with embedding parameters included, models of different depths follow their own curves; remove them and they almost collapse onto one. The embedding layer is not small—roughly 600 million parameters in GPT-3—and it is trained. The compute formula's omission of it is a side effect, not the reason.

quiz.q: According to the paper, what problem eventually appears when you scale compute optimally?
options: Data grows too slowly, so the model hits a data wall and two power laws cross.
Batch size will exceed the dataset size.
quiz.why: The most compute-efficient training grows data only about as C^{0.26}, but avoiding overfitting needs about C^{0.54}. When data-limited, loss falls more slowly, so L(D(C)) and L(C_{min}) eventually cross. The paper estimates the intersection near 10^{4} PF-days and 10^{12} parameters, and conjectures it may be close to natural language's entropy.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What does a power law look like on log axes? How much does loss drop when parameters grow 10x?
Why does each additional 10x bring a smaller absolute drop in loss? Can loss reach 0?
Where does N ≈ 12 · n_{layer} · d_{model}^{2} come from? Why does training each token take about 6N operations?
Why does the paper say architecture barely matters? In what range does that conclusion hold?
If the model grows 8x, how much should data grow? How does that differ from Chinchilla's conclusion?
Why is training to convergence inefficient? Where does the optimal approach roughly stop?
With 10x more compute, how should model size, data, batch size, and steps change?
What contradiction does the paper identify? What might the intersection point mean?
Where does Chinchilla think this paper got it wrong? Which limitation the paper itself listed does that relate to?
